asDecan.p: Astrologers split each sign into three ten-degree slices called decans, and each slice gets a ruling planet and one of the small cards. Your Sun sits somewhere between ten and nineteen degrees of Sagittarius, the middle slice, and in the Golden Dawn order the Moon rules it. Sagittarius is mutable fire under Jupiter, restless and hopeful and always looking past the next hill. The Moon has no special dignity there. It's a guest in the house, neither helped nor held back, and it picks up Jupiter's manners while it stays. What it brings is memory and feeling, and a need for somewhere to come back to. The Eight of Wands before you is Mercury's slice, all speed. The Ten after you is Saturn's, where the load gets heavy. You're in the middle, where the sign is at full strength and has already been knocked about a bit. Temperance is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You're the friend who says yes to the road trip and then quietly packs a first-aid kit, a spare charger and snacks for everyone. Sagittarius wants to go, and the Moon remembers what happened last time. At a family dinner you're warm and loud and telling stories, and you also clock the moment your sister goes quiet, and you'll bring it up with her later on the phone. When a plan you were excited about falls through, you're fine about it in public for about a day. Then on a Sunday with nothing planned it catches up with you, and you're surprisingly low. Your mood follows your sense of whether life is going somewhere. Give you a trip booked for March, even a small one, and you'll put up with a lot of rubbish at work in the meantime.

The less obvious thing you're good at is staying. Plenty of Sagittarians are brilliant for the first fortnight of someone's bad patch. You're still ringing in month four, when a friend's divorce has gone dull and everyone else has stopped asking. The Moon keeps track of people, and you'll remember the anniversary of someone's dad dying without writing it down anywhere. You've also got a second wind. In a long project, a renovation that's run six weeks over or a thesis in its final year, there's a point where everyone's sick of it, and that's usually where you find a reason to keep going and talk the others into it too. It isn't cheerleading exactly. You've had worse and you can say so, and people believe you.

What people don't see straight away is how long you hold on to things. You'll forgive someone properly, you mean it, and then two years later in an argument about the dishes, out comes the thing they said at your birthday, word for word. The Moon files everything. The other habit is leaving early. If a job or a friendship starts to feel like it might hurt, you're often the one who books the flight or quietly stops replying, and you'll call it needing space. Sometimes it is. Sometimes you've just decided to go before anyone can make you. You also make a joke of the thing that's actually bothering you, and people laugh along and miss it, and then you're a bit hurt that nobody asked.

When something goes badly, a redundancy, a break-up, a friend who lets you down, the first thing you do is get busy being fine. You make jokes about it at the pub and start looking at flights. That lasts a few days. About a week later it drops on you, usually at night, and you're lying awake going over every hard thing that's ever happened to you, right back to school. The Moon pulls up the whole file. You can get prickly around then, short with your partner, cagey on the phone with your mum, and they're left guessing because a week ago you seemed okay. What helps is plain and physical. Proper sleep, a meal someone else cooked, and one person you tell the true version to early, before the jokes set in.

You come across as easygoing in love, up for anything, happy to split the bill and see where the night goes. Underneath that you're checking whether this person is safe to come home to. You'll want room to go off, a weekend hiking with friends, a month working abroad, and while you're away you miss them more than you let on, sending a photo of a sunset at eleven at night. What hurts you most is being teased about the things you believe in. A partner can mock your cooking all they like, but laugh at the retreat you went on, or the book that changed your mind about something, and you'll go cold for the evening without quite saying why. Tell them which things are off limits. They can't guess.

Work has to mean something to you, and it has to feel like it's heading somewhere, or your energy drains within months. Fields that mix care with distance suit this decan well. Remote-area nursing, aid work, teaching adults, running tours, anything where you look after people who are a long way from home. You're good in the long middle stretch of a job, the second year of a contract when the novelty's gone and the results haven't shown up yet. The trouble is you often end up carrying the team's mood as well as your own workload. In a restructure you're the one colleagues come to for a debrief in the car park, and you'll do it, and go home flat. Keep a clear line between your job and the unofficial one. Nobody's paying you for the second.

At twenty this decan is often restless and a bit bruised. You leave home early or badly, you travel on very little money, and the first few big disappointments land hard because you honestly expected things to go well. By the mid-thirties most people with this slice of Sagittarius have been through enough to stop being shocked by setbacks, and something in them relaxes. You still expect things to work out, you've just got a record of it by then. The guardedness tends to peak around the same time, and plenty of people spend their late thirties learning to let someone help. The fifties are usually good to you. I've seen a lot of these charts turn into the older friend everyone rings in a crisis, partly because you've clearly had your own and you're still cheerful about it.

Keep a short list on your phone with a boring name, like 'done'. Whenever you get through something hard, a bad stretch at work, a hospital visit, a row that got sorted out, add one line with the date. No commentary. When the next rough patch starts and your head begins pulling up every old hurt, open the list instead and read the last five lines. Then text one of the people who got you through one of them, just to say hello.
